title: Katha, the explanation
hookLine: exposition of Gurbani by a teacher

cards: The kirtan stops. The musicians set down their instruments, and one person sits up at the front, near the Granth, without a harmonium. They read a single line of Gurbani aloud, slowly.
Then again. Then they start to talk. Who wrote this line, and what was happening around it.
What this one word means, and why the Guru may have picked it over another. A story from the Gurus' lives. Another line from elsewhere in the Granth that answers this one like an echo.
A long while can pass on one sentence. Children who were fidgeting go still. This is katha.

teach.b: Katha means telling, or a discourse. In the gurdwara it's exposition: a teacher taking a passage of Gurbani and explaining it to the sangat. Kirtan sings the word; katha unfolds it.
The Sikh Rehat Maryada speaks to it directly.

teach.h: ONLY A SIKH, KEEPING TO GURMAT.
teach.b: In paraphrase: in the congregation, only a Sikh may give katha, and the explanation must be in keeping with Gurmat, the Guru's teaching. That's a guardrail.
Katha is an aid to the word, not a stage for the speaker's own opinions dressed up as scripture. Picture the shape of it.

teach.h: THE LINE STAYS ABOVE THE TALK.
teach.b: The Granth stays open, above everyone. The teacher sits lower, facing the people, holding a line up to the light and turning it.
A good explanation doesn't replace the line; it sends you back to it, and now you hear more in it.
Why it matters: Gurbani is poetry, written in old Punjabi and other languages of its time, packed with images of rivers, merchants, brides and fields.

Without someone to unpack them, a listener can sing a hymn for years and miss what it's saying. Katha passes the meaning from one person who has studied to a room full of people who want to understand.
Some teachers speak at length on a single word; others give a short talk before the evening prayer.
Either way, words that were heard are now explained.

how: In gurdwaras a katha may follow the kirtan: a teacher reads a passage of Gurbani and explains its words, setting and meaning to the congregation, while the Guru Granth Sahib remains open above.

o: a reading of the whole Granth without a break
explaining a passage of Gurbani to the sangat
singing hymns with harmonium and tabla

p: only a Sikh, keeping to Gurmat

s: katha is a chance for a speaker to share any opinion

games.q: you've been asked to give katha on one line of Gurbani. what is your job?
o: say what you personally think, whatever it is.
open up the line in keeping with the Guru's teaching.
sing the line again, without speaking.
games.why: the code asks for exposition in keeping with Gurmat. singing is kirtan; katha unfolds what was sung.

practice: Take one word you've met on this path, like Waheguru, and say it once, slowly. Then ask it the katha questions, one at a time: what does each part mean, what picture is in it, where else have you heard something like it?
Don't hurry to an answer; let the word sit above your thoughts and notice what opens.

wordCard.voice: Katha. Telling, discourse: the exposition of Gurbani by a teacher to the sangat, kept in line with the Guru's teaching. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: explained. A good explanation always sends you back to the line. Rest well.
